title: ALPN callback function sometimes leads to segfault in node.js >= 18.13.0
body: I am running Node.js 18.15.0 on Ubuntu Linux and occasionally see my HTTPS server terminate with SIGSEGV inside SSL_select_next_proto, called from SelectALPNCallback while parsing a ClientHello. It is rare, around one request per million, and I have not found a local reproducer. A second production crash had the same stack. I extracted a core dump from Kubernetes, but the release binary does not have the debug symbols I need. I initially suspected a malformed ALPN header or an invalid pointer passed into SSL_select_next_proto. I can add instrumentation or collect more information if someone tells me what to inspect. The server should reject bad input rather than segfault.

symptoms_visible: My Node.js 18.15.0 HTTPS server occasionally exits with SIGSEGV while SSL_select_next_proto is called from SelectALPNCallback during ClientHello processing.
I see roughly one crash per million requests in production and have not reproduced it locally.
N0.label: N0 rare production ALPN crash reported

symptoms_visible: The production process still occasionally crashes at SSL_select_next_proto+76 while reading through a pointer held in rax.
N1.label: N1 crash machine state collected

symptoms_visible: With ALPNProtocols set to an empty array, production core dumps still occur, although I observed them less often than with the default ALPN configuration.
N2_x.label: N2_x empty ALPN workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: The production crash continues, but the ClientHello data recovered from three dumps contains a normal ALPN extension offering h2 and http/1.1.
Replaying the recovered message locally for one million iterations does not crash.
N3.label: N3 malformed ALPN theory ruled out

symptoms_visible: After reverting the production servers to Node.js 18.12.0, I observed zero core dumps across ten servers over the following day; newer versions had been crashing about once per hour with the default ALPN setting.
N4.label: N4 pre-regression version stable in production

symptoms_visible: In a controlled two-connection run, both ALPN callbacks receive the same callback-argument value even though one connection is opened and closed before the other sends its ClientHello.
A separate affected production operator reports that a Node.js 20.8.0 build with the candidate patch no longer exhibits the crash.
N5.label: N5 shared callback argument demonstrated and patch tested

symptoms_visible: One affected production operator reports no recurrence when running a build containing the callback-lifetime fix, but the original reporter has not reported a retest on that deployment and later users have reported possible TLS crashes on released builds.
N_terminal.label: terminal patch landed without original reporter verification

question_patterns: Can you run disassemble and info registers for the top SSL_select_next_proto frame in the core dump?
At the faulting instruction, what are the register values and which instruction is crashing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The fault is always at SSL_select_next_proto+76, `movzbl (%rax),%eax`. In this dump rax, rdx and rdi are all 0x75684f4f7156766e, while r8/r15 point to 0x7f499574c150 and r9/r14 are 12. I pasted the full disassembly and register output.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The crash is actually in memcmp after both ALPN buffers have been read successfully, and every pointer is mapped and stable.
The fault is the same dereference in SSL_select_next_proto, but the invalid address differs between core dumps.

question_patterns: Can you provide a hex dump of the top 32 or 64 bytes of the stack for the OpenSSL and callback frames?
Please dump the stack memory around the SSL_select_next_proto and SelectALPNCallback frames.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I dumped both frames. The OpenSSL frame contains the saved callback return address and the next frame, and the callback frame has saved rip 0x1834f83. I pasted the `x/16wx` and `x/8xw` output.

edges.comment: Messages c2-c5, reporter's Node 18.15 production core: participant1 requested disassembly, registers, and stack bytes; the reporter supplied raw GDB output.

solution.intent: Avoid the crash by disabling server-side ALPN negotiation with an empty ALPNProtocols array.
solution.concrete_example: Set `ALPNProtocols: []` in the options passed to `https.createServer()` and monitor whether the production crashes stop.

edges.comment: Messages c9-c11 and c24 describe the reporter's HTTPS server. The reporter initially said an empty ALPN list solved the issue, but later production evidence showed core dumps still occurred every few hours. Participant8 independently confirmed in c44 that this setting did not resolve the crash.

question_patterns: Can you recover and share the TLS handshake bytes that were being processed when the server crashed?
Please decode the ClientHello from the crash and report the raw ALPN extension contents.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I recovered and decoded the ClientHello. The ALPN extension is `0010 000e 000c 02 6832 08 687474702f312e31`, offering `h2` and `http/1.1`. I checked three dumps and all three have a valid ALPN record. I also replayed the full recovered message locally in a loop for one million iterations without a failure.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The crashing ClientHello contains a zero-length ALPN protocol list that violates the expected encoding, and replaying those exact bytes crashes reliably.
The captured ALPN list offers only http/1.1 rather than h2 and http/1.1, but it is still correctly encoded and replay does not crash.

edges.comment: Messages c13-c20, reporter's production dump: maintainers requested handshake bytes; the reporter recovered and decoded a complete ClientHello, found valid ALPN in three dumps, and could not reproduce the crash by replaying it. The local replay result is recorded as volunteered information.

question_patterns: Can you deploy a version from before the regression window and report whether the production core dumps continue?
Please compare the affected release with Node.js 18.12 under the same production workload.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reverted to Node.js 18.12.0. Since yesterday there have been zero core dumps across ten production servers. With the default ALPN setting on newer Node versions I had been getting about one dump per hour. I attached the code-change screenshot that led me to test this boundary.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Node.js 18.12 crashes at the same rate and with the same SSL_select_next_proto stack.
Node.js 18.12 remains stable on eight servers rather than ten during the same observation period.

question_patterns: Which source change or version boundary made you choose Node.js 18.12 for the comparison?
When did this behavior first appear relative to the ALPN callback changes?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The crashes start with versions after 18.12, and I found the `src: optimize ALPN callback` change introduced for 18.13. Reverting to the version before that change is what made production stable.

solution.intent: Use Node.js 18.12 as a temporary production mitigation while diagnosing the ALPN callback lifetime regression introduced in later versions.
solution.concrete_example: Temporarily deploy Node.js 18.12.x, monitor the same production traffic for core dumps, and retain the crash artifacts for diagnosing the newer ALPN implementation.

edges.comment: Messages c20-c24 concern the original reporter's production deployment. Installing and retaining 18.12 is a persistent system change, so this is mixed rather than a measurement-only edge. The attached c22 image accompanies the reporter's explanation of the source-version boundary.

question_patterns: Can you inspect the callback argument for two overlapping TLS connections and report the raw values seen by each callback?
Please break in SelectALPNCallback while interleaving two connections and compare the callback-argument register values.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I opened connection A, waited, opened B, sent B's ClientHello, closed B, waited, and then sent A's ClientHello. With GDB breaking in SelectALPNCallback, both callbacks had the same value in r9, which is the callback argument stored on SSL_CTX.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Each overlapping connection receives a distinct callback argument that continues to point to its own live TLS object.
The same callback-argument value is observed with shorter delays between the two connections.

question_patterns: Can an affected production operator test the candidate build under representative traffic and report whether the same crash recurs?
Please deploy the candidate build to an affected workload and monitor for the SSL_select_next_proto crash.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: We tested the candidate fix on an affected Node.js 20.8.0 production workload and can confirm that the crash stopped occurring.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The candidate build continues to crash at SSL_select_next_proto under the same production load.

edges.comment: The first answer comes from participant7's affected production system and controlled GDB experiment in c33-c43; the second comes from participant8's affected production workload in c44-c45. These affected operators are folded into the simulated user side, but neither result is represented as the original reporter's own final verification.

solution.intent: Fix the ALPN callback lifetime bug by obtaining the TLSWrap for the current SSL connection instead of storing a per-connection TLSWrap pointer as callback state on the shared SSL_CTX; then ask the original reporter to verify a build containing that fix under production load.
solution.concrete_example: Change SelectALPNCallback so it recovers the TLSWrap associated with the current `SSL*` connection, rather than dereferencing a TLSWrap pointer retained in the shared SSL_CTX callback argument. Test a build containing that change under the affected production workload and confirm that the SSL_select_next_proto crashes no longer recur.
solution.inference_hint: The raw GDB experiment only establishes that overlapping connections receive the same SSL_CTX callback argument. The engineering conclusion is that the ALPN optimization moved a per-connection TLSWrap pointer onto a shared SSL_CTX; another connection can replace that pointer and then be garbage-collected, leaving a stale callback argument. Recovering TLSWrap from the current SSL object restores per-connection lifetime ownership.

edges.comment: Final accepted diagnosis is developed in c33-c43 and implemented by the linked candidate fix, with production confirmation from participant8 in c45. The original reporter never confirmed the landed fix on their own deployment, and later commenters c48-c49 reported possible persistence, so the graph does not claim reporter-verified resolution.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: a per-connection TLSWrap pointer was stored as the ALPN callback argument on a shared SSL_CTX, allowing another connection and object lifetime or garbage-collection timing to leave the callback with a stale pointer.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the production-only version boundary, valid captured ALPN records, the invalid pointer at SSL_select_next_proto, and the two-connection GDB observation that both callbacks receive the same SSL_CTX callback argument.
The corrective approach must recover the TLSWrap from the current SSL connection rather than retaining a child connection pointer on the shared SSL_CTX.
Must not present malformed or empty ALPN input as the final root cause, and must not present ALPNProtocols: [] as the fix because crashes continued with that configuration.
A downgrade to Node.js 18.12 may be offered only as a temporary mitigation, not as the permanent fix.

Must ask the original reporter to verify a build containing the fix under representative production load before declaring the original case resolved; another operator's successful candidate-build test is supporting evidence, not the reporter's own confirmation.

persona_hint.experience_level: Production Node.js operator who can extract Kubernetes core dumps, use GDB, decode raw TLS ClientHello bytes, build or downgrade Node.js, and run stress tests, but describes their C++ and assembly knowledge as limited.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, evidence-driven, and candid about uncertainty; posts raw crash data and incremental findings, tests suggestions in production when necessary, and revises initial hypotheses when captures contradict them.
